extracted.intended_audience: readers and scholars of early Pacific exploration, colonial administrators, and students of historical voyage narratives
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive standards embedded in a voyage narrative for claiming territory, founding a municipal government, organizing religious and civic ceremonies, conducting expeditions, and assessing a port/land for settlement and naval use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ceremony for claiming land in the sovereign's name
rubrics_metrics.description: To take possession of newly discovered lands in the King's name: a formal proclamation is read naming the place, the royal standard is hoisted, Masses are said, banners and ensigns are presented before the altar and blessed, and ships and soldiers fire salutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Textual examples: the proclamation naming 'Australia del Espiritu Santo' in the name of the King; three Masses (the fourth sung by the Father Commissary); Ensigns inclined before the altar and blessed; ships firing guns with full charges, soldiers discharging muskets and arquebuses, gunners sending off rockets and fire-wheels; public cries of 'Long live the King...' and 'Long live the Faith of Christ!'. These ceremonial acts serve as the formal legal/religious claim and public confirmation of possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founding a municipality and election of magistrates
rubrics_metrics.description: When possession is taken and a site is to become a city (capital of a province), senior officers (Captain, Master of the Camp, Admiral, Ensign, Sergeant-Major, Captains) assemble to elect a municipality and officers 'as is usual in a city that was the capital of a province.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure shown: concurrence among senior officers, agreement on the manner of elections, and a full slate of named offices (magistrates, secretaries, justices, chief constable, royal officers such as accountant, treasurer, factor, registrar of mines, store-keeper general, overseer). The narrative lists specific persons and offices as an exemplar of the expected municipal structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oath-taking procedure for municipal officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Immediately after election, municipal officials take an oath placing the right hand on a breviary held by the Father Commissary and swear loyalty to His Majesty in whose name the offices are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oath ritual (hand on breviary, Father Commissary present) is presented as a required legitimizing act completing the proceedings; this is the formal mechanism for binding officials to the Crown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing major religious processions (Corpus Christi example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prescribed order and set of elements for a major procession: ceremonial objects (heavy cross, gilt cross, coffer with the sacrament), sequence of participants (soldier, lay brother, acolytes, companies with banners and drums, dancers, magistrates with torches, Father Commissary under a pall), music and dancing, bell-ringing and gun salutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed ordering: soldier carrying heavy cross first; lay brother with cross; acolytes with candlesticks and red cassocks; three companies with banners and drums; sword-dance by sailors and dances by boys; royal standard accompanied by Master of the Camp and captains; magistrates with torches; Father Commissary with a yellow silk pall borne by officers; coffer of crimson velvet with the sacrament incensed and carried; bells and artillery fired on the Lord's coming forth. Decorations (arches, palms, flowers) and feeding/festivities afterwards are part of the successful celebration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manumission practice in the field
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for granting freedom to slaves encountered during the expedition: slave-owners (officers) draw up letters of manumission and formally free their slaves, often motivated by pious reasons or the honour of a festival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: two officers each freed a slave and 'drew up letters' to effect freedom; it was done publicly in the context of a festival and described as an act motivated by pious motives and honour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline, justice, and punishment aboard expedition
rubrics_metrics.description: The captain's approach to discipline includes informing, pardoning, giving hope, imprisonment as punishment, and corporal punishment (rod) calibrated to the offence; secret intentions are ultimately left to God but visible acts must justify treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative notes: Captain justified his use of information, pardon, hope, imprisonment, or rod blows depending on circumstances; he kept the Chief Pilot prisoner as sufficient punishment where appropriate. The account emphasizes proportionality, public evidence, and the Captain's view of honour and trustworthiness as factors in disciplinary decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconnaissance and expeditionary tactics inland
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines for inland reconnaissance: send a suitably armed party (e.g., Master of the Camp with thirty soldiers), post spies before landing, probe heights and valleys, test river mouths with boats and launches, and be prepared to retreat and call for naval support if met with superior native force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reconnaissance of a height and valley with a 30-man party encountering villages and ambuscades; posting two spies who warned the natives; using launches to sound river mouths (oar+arm depth test), landing to examine villages, and retiring when drums and many people were heard. Tactical measures included firing guns to frighten natives, rearguard/ship support, and rapid coordination between shore and ship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishing agriculture and testing land fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: To test land suitability for settlement, sow seeds of familiar European crops (maize, cotton, onions, melons, pumpkins, beans, pulse) and observe sprouting and yields as an early gauge of fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative: the Captain sowed a variety of seeds and later reported seeing them sprouting; such field trials are presented as practical tests of the land's capacity to support colonists and supply ships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall criteria for assessing land and port suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable site combines fertile soil, a good port with a river, abundant forests and quarries, clay for tiles and bricks, level lands near hills, capacity for dockyards, nearby islands, and capacity to sustain many settlers with local resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's summary: the port described is 'more delightful, healthy and fertile' than others; he lists advantages such as quarries, timber, clay for tiles and bricks, a river and port on a plain, forests for ship timbers, and the nearby seven islands. The narrative explicitly contrasts this site favorably against known ports like Acapulco, Panama, and others, giving reasons why it would make a principal settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harbour and anchorage technical criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific navigational and harbour metrics: bay circuit and entrance width, latitude/longitude, compass variation, depth soundings (fathoms), suitability for boats and frigates, bottom composition (black sand), lack of reefs/banks, anchorage depths (capacity cited up to '40½ brazas'), and safer approach points (e.g., nearer a river mouth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete data in text: the bay has a circuit of 20 leagues, entrance 4 leagues, port at 15°10′ S, compass variation 7° N.E.; river mouth depths measured with an oar and arm; bottom 'black sand' judged clean; room for ships up to specified depth; recommendation to approach near the river Salvador. These are used as practical criteria for safe anchorage and ship operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resources for shipbuilding, dockyards, and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the availability of timber suitable for futtock timbers, houses, compass timbers, beams, planks, masts and yards; quarries and marble or jasper for building; clay for tiles and bricks; fibres and materials for ropes and sails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative details: trees straight and high, abundant forests, examples of uses (planks, lances, sails made from leaves, fibres for caulking and ropes), possible quarries of good marble and jasper, black clay pots, and comment that no better forests or dockyard resources had been seen. These material resources are presented as central to a port's utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustenance and provisioning criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess local food and provisioning potential by presence and abundance of edible roots/tubers, domestic pigs (size and numbers), fowl, wild game and birds, fish species, fruits (coconuts, plantains, obos, almonds, nuts, oranges), and materials for food preservation (fish/flesh salting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: locals grew roots eaten like potatoes, large pigs (one 200 lbs), many fowls, fish (skate, sole, pollack, red mullet, pargos, sardines), fruits and sugarcane suitable for sugar, coconut uses (wine, oil, honey, balsam), and the note that roots kept well while voyaging. Caveat example: pargos considered poisonous causing nausea/fever among those who ate them. These factors determine whether a port can provision ships and settlers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climate and public health indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators of a healthy, clement climate suitable for settlement include: clear fresh rivers, pleasant mornings and afternoons, little rain and thunder, absence of mosquitos and ants, lack of poisonous lizards/alligators, presence of many old people among the natives, and trees unbroken by storms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's observations used as diagnostic signs: no mosquitos/ants seen; no snow on mountains; many old people indicating longevity; clear rivers meaning rains likely past; straight unbroken trees implying absence of great storms; fish and flesh keep well for salting. These are used to judge whether a place is healthy for long-term habitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Native population and cultural/economic indicators for settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the indigenous population's characteristics (corpulent, clean, fond of festivities), housing and agriculture (wooden houses with palm roofs, terraces, gardens, root crops), artisanship (pots, looms, worked marble/jasper), weapons (wooden clubs, bows, reed arrows), burial customs, musical instruments, and potential local extraction (reported metal/ore).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative data: natives weave cloths, keep food clean, use musical instruments, practice dances, maintain burial oratories and figures; households store food in outhouses; evidence of pottery, looms, mother-of-pearl, ebony, and a heap of black stones later identified as ore with possible silver extraction. These items inform assessments of whether the local population can supply labour, goods, or resources and how they may interact with settlers.
